questions.topic: Row vs Columnar Layout: Which Workload Wins
questions.question: In a columnar storage layout, which bytes are stored contiguously on disk?
options: All fields of a single record, laid out in schema order
All values of a single column, across a large batch of rows
All rows that share the same primary key prefix, grouped together
All distinct values of every column, sorted in ascending order

questions.topic: Row vs Columnar Layout: Which Workload Wins
questions.question: Which access pattern is the classic case where a row-oriented layout beats a columnar one?
options: Scanning two numeric columns across a billion rows to compute an average
Filtering a large table on a date range and aggregating one measure
Compressing a table whose columns contain many repeated values
Fetching and updating one complete record by its key at high frequency

questions.topic: Row vs Columnar Layout: Which Workload Wins
questions.question: A 20 GB table has 50 columns of roughly equal width. A query filters and aggregates using only 2 of them. Roughly how much raw data must each layout read?
options: About 0.8 GB with a columnar layout versus about 20 GB with a row layout
About 10 GB with a columnar layout versus about 20 GB with a row layout
About 0.8 GB with a columnar layout versus about 2 GB with a row layout
About 2 GB with either layout, since the filter bounds what gets read

questions.topic: Row vs Columnar Layout: Which Workload Wins
questions.question: You are designing storage for a service that reads and rewrites one user profile at a time at high QPS. Which choice fits the workload?
options: Columnar, because repeated profile fields will compress extremely well
Columnar, because vectorized execution accelerates every kind of read
Row-oriented, because each profile is one contiguous read and write
Row-oriented, because column statistics make key lookups nearly free

questions.topic: Row vs Columnar Layout: Which Workload Wins
questions.question: An analyst runs `SELECT *` on a 200-column columnar table to fetch the single row for one order ID, and it is far slower than the same lookup in a row store. Why?
options: Because the filter on the order ID cannot be evaluated until every row group is fully decompressed
Because columnar files store keys separately from values, forcing two passes over the table
Because the record must be reassembled from 200 separate column locations instead of one contiguous read
Because `SELECT *` disables the query planner and forces an unindexed full-table sort

questions.topic: Row vs Columnar Layout: Which Workload Wins
questions.question: A pipeline writes a few hundred events to a columnar file every few seconds, and analysts complain scans are slow. Which property of columnar formats is being violated?
options: Columnar formats require rows to arrive pre-sorted by their primary key
Columnar formats are batch-oriented and need many rows laid out together for their I/O and compression benefits
Columnar formats only support append operations from a single writer at a time
Columnar formats require every column to have the same fixed byte width

questions.topic: Parquet Row Groups and Column Chunks
questions.question: In a Parquet file, what is a row group?
options: A set of rows that share identical values in the partition column
A compressed page of values belonging to exactly one column
An index structure mapping each row's key to its byte offset
A horizontal slice of the table containing one column chunk per column

questions.topic: Parquet Row Groups and Column Chunks
questions.question: Where does a Parquet reader find the schema and the byte offsets of every column chunk?
options: In the footer metadata at the end of the file, which it reads first
In a header block at the start of the file, before any row groups
In a separate sidecar index file written alongside the data file
In the first page of each column chunk, decoded during the scan

questions.topic: Parquet Row Groups and Column Chunks
questions.question: A query needs 2 of 40 columns from a Parquet file with 80 row groups stored on object storage. What does an efficient reader actually fetch?
options: The whole file once, since object storage only supports full-object reads
The footer, then byte-range reads covering the 160 needed column chunks
The first row group in full, then only the matching pages of the rest
The footer, then the first page of all 3,200 column chunks to check types

questions.topic: Parquet Row Groups and Column Chunks
questions.question: A writer was configured to produce 5,000-row row groups on a billion-row table. Which symptom should you expect?
options: Readers cannot parallelize because the file has too few split points
The writer runs out of memory buffering each row group before flushing
Footer metadata and per-chunk overhead balloon while compression weakens
Column statistics become unusable because groups are too small to record min and max

questions.topic: Parquet Row Groups and Column Chunks
questions.question: A 2 GB Parquet file was written as a single row group. On a busy cluster, one task processes it while other workers sit idle. Why?
options: The row group is the unit of splitting, so one row group cannot be divided across tasks
The footer can only be held by one reader at a time, serializing all access to the file
Files above 1 GB disable parallel reads to protect object storage rate limits
The column chunks are compressed, and compressed data can only be read sequentially

questions.topic: Parquet Row Groups and Column Chunks
questions.question: After raising the row group target from 128 MB to 1 GB, an ingestion job starts running out of memory. What explains this?
options: Larger row groups force the writer to keep multiple copies of the footer in memory
Larger row groups require the reader's schema to be revalidated on every flush
Larger row groups multiply the number of pages that must be tracked per column
The writer buffers an entire row group in memory before it can flush to storage

questions.question: Which statistics does a Parquet writer record for each column chunk to enable data skipping?
options: A histogram of value frequencies and the top ten most common values
The mean, variance, and standard deviation of the chunk's values
A sorted list of every distinct value that appears in the chunk
The minimum value, maximum value, and count of nulls in the chunk

questions.question: What does predicate pushdown with min/max statistics let a scan do?
options: Rewrite the query plan so filters run after aggregation completes
Skip entire row groups whose statistics prove no row can match the filter
Return approximate results by sampling one page per column chunk
Evaluate filters inside the storage service before bytes reach the network

questions.question: A filter `WHERE user_id = 'u-93f2'` on a randomly shuffled UUID column skips zero row groups even though statistics are present and correct. Why?
options: Because equality predicates can never be evaluated against min/max statistics
Because UUID columns are stored as binary, and binary chunks carry no statistics
Because every row group's min and max span nearly the whole value range, so no group can be proven empty of matches
Because pushdown only applies to numeric columns and silently ignores strings

questions.question: After sorting a table by `event_ts` before writing, a timestamp-range dashboard query gets roughly 20x cheaper with no query changes. What changed?
options: Each row group now covers a narrow, nearly disjoint time range, so most groups fail the min/max overlap test and are skipped
Sorting shrank the file so much that the entire table now fits in the scan cache
Sorted data lets the engine binary-search inside pages instead of scanning them
The sort rewrote the footer so that statistics are now stored per page instead of per chunk

questions.question: A row group passes the min/max check for `WHERE amount = 500` but turns out to contain no row with amount 500. What happens?
options: The engine returns a wrong result unless a checksum catches the mismatch
The group is read and the filter drops every row; stats prove absence, never presence, so this is wasted I/O but a correct answer
The engine marks the file's statistics as corrupt and disables pruning for the table
The scan falls back to a full-table read because the statistics contradicted the data

questions.question: Which predicate is least likely to benefit from min/max row-group pruning?
options: An equality match on a column the table was sorted by at write time
A range condition on a timestamp column with clustered values
An `IS NULL` check on a column whose chunks record null counts
A not-equals condition on a column whose values span a wide range
